title: Decay of December anomalies cut sea-level forecast error against fixed carry at 217 gauges in 2010-2024
abstract: We tested whether a December sea-level anomaly should decay in forecasts of the next calendar year. We used a fixed PSMSL monthly archive, 217 gauges and 15 target years in 2010-2024. Each fit used the prior 20 years. A first-order decay model reduced mean squared error by 55.66% against carrying the anomaly unchanged. The conditional 95% three-year block limits were 42.75% to 64.39%. Against a trend and seasonal model that ignored the anomaly, the gain was 1.24%, with limits of -0.91% to 3.34%. Equal geographic cell weighting gave a 3.37% baseline gain, with limits of 1.19% to 5.23%. Thus decay avoided large fixed-carry errors, but added value depended on the comparator and weighting. Complete-origin and training-window checks preserved the gain over fixed carry. The method is established; this study adds a paired benchmark for this sample and period. Revised data, uneven coverage, December-only origins, short tests and conditional intervals limit inference. We do not identify a physical recovery process. The package contains original code, aggregate evidence, source hashes, an audit and a figure. Source records and record-level outputs remain external.

display.caption: Decay-model MSE reduction against fixed carry and the trend and seasonal baseline. Limits use three-year blocks shared across gauges. Positive values mean lower error. Quarter and lead time change together.

citations.reason: Prior seasonal-change benchmark informed this new anomaly-decay question and source selection. Source records overlap; this is not independent confirmation.
